1-1-1.explanation: The supplied NET source presents the Bhagavad Gita as a psychological-spiritual framework centred on action, self-knowledge and disciplined engagement with duty. Karma Yoga emphasises action without performance anxiety or attachment to the fruits of action; the broader Gita framework also links works, knowledge and devotion. A key exam distinction is The key NET distinction is not simply 'do your duty'. The source connects action with reduced attachment to outcomes and places Karma Yoga alongside knowledge and devotion as complementary paths. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are duty/action without attachment to fruits, Jnanayoga, Bhakti Yoga, equanimity and self-knowledge.

1-1-2.title: Buddhism
1-1-2.explanation: The supplied NET source presents Buddhism through the problem of suffering and the route toward its cessation. The Four Noble Truths identify suffering, its cause in craving/attachment, the possibility of cessation, and the path toward cessation; the Eightfold Path is described as a Middle Way between indulgence and severe asceticism. A key exam distinction is Do not reduce Buddhism in this syllabus to a list of moral rules. The exam-relevant structure is a causal sequence: suffering → its source → possibility of cessation → path. For exam application, When a stem asks for the truth concerning cessation or the path to cessation, distinguish Nirodha from Magga. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are Eightfold Path / Middle Way, nirvana.

1-2-1.title: Pre-independence era
1-2-1.explanation: Formal psychology education in India began in the early 20th century within a colonial education system. The uploaded NET material traces an important institutional beginning to Calcutta University: Sir Asutosh Mukherjee promoted Experimental Psychology in the postgraduate curriculum; Brojendra Nath Seal prepared the 1905 syllabus and established a laboratory. The laboratory was later upgraded into the first Department of Experimental Psychology. Research there included depth perception, psychophysics and attention. Psychology was included as a separate section of the Indian Science Congress in 1923; the Indian Psychological Association was founded in 1924 and the Indian Journal of Psychology appeared in 1925. 1-2-2.title: Post-independence era
1-2-2.explanation: The source describes post-independence psychology as expanding institutionally while remaining strongly influenced by its philosophical and Western scientific inheritance. After 1947, psychology was linked with nation-building and research. Departments expanded in universities such as Mysore and Patna; the University Grants Commission, established in 1956, supported university development. Applied and clinical psychology also expanded through institutions including NCERT and mental-health centres. The source notes that many psychology departments had emerged from philosophy departments, creating a continuing tension between philosophical roots and the aspiration to establish psychology as an experimental science. 1-2-3.title: 1970s social issues
1-2-3.explanation: During the 1970s, the source describes a shift toward socially relevant psychological research. Concerns included communal violence, social conflict and problems that were difficult to understand through culturally neutral laboratory approaches alone. The UNESCO-supported work associated with Gardner Murphy investigated communal violence and culminated in the 1953 volume In the Minds of Men; the later historical account presents this tradition as part of psychology's growing engagement with Indian social problems. The period also contributed to criticism that psychology should address the realities of Indian society rather than simply reproduce Western research. 1-2-6.title: 1990s disciplinary identity crisis
1-2-6.explanation: The source describes a disciplinary identity crisis in Indian psychology emerging strongly in the 1970s–1990s debate. Review of Indian research led scholars to question whether psychology had become largely imitative of Western research and insufficiently responsive to Indian social reality. Nandy and Agrawal are cited in this criticism, while D. Sinha called for indigenous psychology using Indian concepts and theories. J. B. P. Sinha's distinction between the 'bulk' and 'front' of research captures the uneven response: much research remained imitative, while some psychologists increasingly took indigenous psychology seriously. 1-2-7.title: 2000s Indian psychology in academia
1-2-7.explanation: The source marks the 2000s as a period in which Indian psychology became more explicitly articulated within academic discussion. A major source example is the 2002 National Conference on Yoga and Indian Approaches to Psychology in Pondicherry, where participants issued the Manifesto on Indian Psychology. For NET preparation, the important point is the historical continuity between philosophical inquiry and the later emergence of psychology as a distinct discipline. A key exam distinction is Do not treat Greek heritage as experimental psychology. Its relevance here is historical: philosophical questions about mind and knowledge predate psychology's institutional emergence as an independent science. For exam application, When a question asks about the philosophical roots of psychology rather than laboratory psychology, retrieve the Greek heritage context.

1-4-2.title: Medieval period
1-4-2.explanation: The supplied NET material places the medieval period within the longer intellectual history preceding modern psychology. The period is important for understanding how questions concerning soul, knowledge, morality and human nature continued to be treated within philosophical and religious frameworks before psychology became an independent experimental discipline. A key exam distinction is The NET distinction is historical rather than methodological: medieval thought belongs to the pre-disciplinary history of ideas about mind and human nature, not to modern experimental psychology. For exam application, If the question asks about psychology's intellectual development before its establishment as an independent science, place medieval thought in this historical sequence. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are medieval intellectual history, soul and mind, moral/religious frameworks, pre-scientific psychology.

1-5-1.title: Structuralism
1-5-1.explanation: Structuralism treated conscious experience as something that could be analysed into basic elements, using introspection as its central method. Edward Titchener is the key NET association; he brought structuralism to the United States. A key exam distinction is Structuralism asks what conscious experience is made of; functionalism asks what mental processes do and how they help adaptation. Wundt's work and Titchener's structuralism should not be treated as identical. For exam application, A question describes analysing conscious experience into elementary components through introspection. Identify the school and theorist before looking at the options. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are elements of conscious experience, analysis of mental structure.

1-5-2.title: Functionalism
1-5-2.explanation: Functionalism shifted attention from analysing the contents of consciousness to the functions of mental activity and behaviour. William James is the central association. The approach asks how mind and behaviour help people function, adapt and respond to their surroundings. A key exam distinction is Functionalism is not the search for the elements of consciousness. That emphasis belongs to structuralism. James was interested in how consciousness operates in real life and in adaptation. For exam application, If a PYQ asks which school is concerned with how the mind helps a person adapt, think William James and functionalism as the first retrieval cue. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are functions of mind, everyday functioning.

1-5-3.title: Psychoanalytical psychology
1-5-3.explanation: Psychoanalytical psychology, as presented in the supplied sources, centres on unconscious processes, conflict and the influence of repressed wishes and experiences on behaviour. Freud's model includes id, ego and superego; psychoanalysis aims to bring repressed unconscious material into consciousness and develop insight. A key exam distinction is Do not confuse repression with rationalization. Repression removes threatening material from conscious awareness, whereas rationalization supplies a rational-sounding explanation for a failure or transgression. For exam application, If a stem describes symptoms as indirect expressions of repressed wishes or asks about bringing unconscious material into consciousness, retrieve the psychoanalytic framework. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are id, ego, superego, pleasure principle.

1-5-4.title: Gestalt psychology
1-5-4.explanation: Gestalt psychology argues that psychological experience, especially perception, cannot always be understood by simply adding isolated sensory elements. The organised pattern or whole matters. Wertheimer, Koffka and Köhler are central figures. A key exam distinction is The key contrast is whole versus isolated elements. Structuralism analyses elements; Gestalt psychology emphasizes the organisation and pattern in which those elements are experienced. For exam application, When a question describes a melody, visual pattern or apparent movement whose experience depends on the relationship among parts, identify the Gestalt principle rather than an element-by-element analysis. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are organized whole, pattern/configuration, insight learning.

1-5-5.title: Behaviorism
1-5-5.explanation: Behaviorism redirected psychology toward observable behaviour and away from treating private consciousness as the primary scientific object. John B. Watson is the central founding figure in the classical school; later behaviourism developed conditioning and reinforcement traditions. 2-2-8.title: Null and alternative hypotheses
2-2-8.explanation: A null hypothesis (H0) states the no-effect, no-difference or specified population relationship assumed for statistical testing. The alternative hypothesis (H1/Ha) states the competing effect or difference; it may be directional (one-tailed) or non-directional (two-tailed). Evidence is evaluated against H0 rather than proving H1 with certainty.

2-2-9.title: Type I and Type II errors
2-2-9.explanation: A Type I error occurs when a true null hypothesis is rejected (false positive); its probability is alpha. A Type II error occurs when a false null hypothesis is not rejected (false negative); its probability is beta. Statistical power is 1−beta, the probability of detecting an effect when it exists.

2-2-10.explanation: Sampling is the procedure for selecting participants or observations from a target population. Sampling method affects representativeness and generalisability.

2-14-6.explanation: A main effect is the effect of one independent variable on the dependent variable averaged across the levels of other factors. 2-14-7.title: Post-hoc comparisons
2-14-7.explanation: Post-hoc comparisons are follow-up tests used after an omnibus analysis indicates differences among multiple group means. They identify which groups differ while controlling the increased familywise Type I error associated with repeated comparisons. They differ from planned contrasts, which are specified before examining the results.

2-16-2.title: One-way ANOVA
2-16-2.explanation: One-way ANOVA examines the effect of one categorical independent variable (factor) with two or more levels on a quantitative dependent variable. It partitions variability into between-groups and within-groups components and tests their mean-square ratio. Follow-up comparisons are needed to locate differences after a significant omnibus result.

A factorial design therefore answers more than separate one-factor comparisons.

3-3-5.explanation: Reliability concerns the consistency or precision of test scores. Test–retest reliability examines stability over time; alternate-forms reliability compares equivalent forms; split-half and internal-consistency estimates examine agreement among items; inter-rater reliability examines agreement between scorers. Reliability is necessary but does not by itself establish validity.

3-4-7.title: Binet-Simon and Stanford-Binet

Do not treat the original and revised scales as identical editions.

They provide an overall intelligence score and index or subtest scores representing different cognitive abilities. Their profile approach allows examination of relative strengths and weaknesses, not merely a single global score.

3-4-9.title: Rorschach
3-4-9.explanation: The Rorschach is a projective personality assessment using a series of inkblot stimuli; the person describes what each blot might represent. Interpretation focuses on features of responses under a structured scoring system. It is distinct from objective inventories because responses are open-ended, and conclusions depend heavily on administration, scoring and validity evidence.

3-4-10.title: Thematic Apperception Test
3-4-10.explanation: The Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), associated with Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan, presents ambiguous pictures and asks the person to make stories. Themes, needs, interpersonal relations and perceived outcomes are interpreted as clues to underlying motives and concerns. Unlike the Rorschach inkblots, TAT stimuli are picture scenes that invite narrative construction.

It is not a projective test and should not be interpreted from one scale in isolation.

4-2-1.title: Neuron structure
4-2-1.explanation: A neuron is a specialised information-processing and information-transmitting cell. Its major structural regions are the soma (cell body), dendrites, axon and terminal buttons. Dendrites generally receive incoming information, the soma maintains the cell and integrates inputs, and the axon carries the neural message toward terminal regions. A key exam distinction is Dendrites and axons have different typical directions of information flow: dendrites receive toward the cell body, whereas the axon carries the neural message away toward terminals. Myelin insulates axons and can increase conduction speed. For exam application, For a structure-function question, map the part to its role: dendrite = receiving, soma = cell body, axon = conducting, terminal = communicating with the next cell. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are axon terminals.

4-2-1.detailed_explanation:
CORE IDEA
A neuron is a specialised information-processing and information-transmitting cell. Its major structural regions are the soma (cell body), dendrites, axon and terminal buttons. Dendrites generally receive incoming information, the soma maintains the cell and integrates inputs, and the axon carries the neural message toward terminal regions.

WHAT TO HOLD IN MEMORY
• soma
• dendrites
• axon
• axon terminals
• myelin

WHAT NOT TO CONFUSE
Dendrites and axons have different typical directions of information flow: dendrites receive toward the cell body, whereas the axon carries the neural message away toward terminals. Myelin insulates axons and can increase conduction speed.

APPLICATION

4-2-3.explanation: Neurons can be distinguished by their role in information flow. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry information toward the central nervous system, motor (efferent) neurons carry commands away from the CNS to effectors, and interneurons connect neural pathways within the CNS. The exam-relevant terms and relationships to retain are sensory/afferent, motor/efferent.

4-2-4.title: Neural impulse
4-2-4.explanation: Neural signalling within an axon depends on changes in membrane potential. At rest the neuron maintains a resting potential; sufficient stimulation reaches threshold and initiates an action potential. Depolarization is followed by repolarization and a refractory phase. A key exam distinction is An action potential is not graded in amplitude: once threshold is reached, the action potential follows an all-or-none pattern. In myelinated axons, saltatory conduction makes the signal appear to jump between nodes of Ranvier. For exam application, When a question asks what happens after threshold, retrieve the sequence: depolarization → repolarization → refractory period.

4-2-5.title: Synaptic transmission
4-2-5.explanation: Communication between neurons occurs across a synapse rather than by direct physical continuity. An action potential reaching the axon terminal triggers processes that allow neurotransmitter substances to be released into the synaptic cleft and influence the receiving cell. A key exam distinction is Neural impulse refers to electrical signalling within the neuron; synaptic transmission concerns communication from one cell to another across the synaptic gap. Do not treat these as identical processes. For exam application, If a stem moves from an action potential at the terminal to release of a chemical messenger and its effect on another cell, the tested concept is synaptic transmission.

4-4-6.title: Spinal cord and autonomic nervous system
4-4-6.explanation: The spinal cord carries sensory information to the brain and motor commands from the brain, and coordinates spinal reflexes. The autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary visceral activity; its sympathetic division mobilises the body during demand, while the parasympathetic division supports restoration and energy conservation. The divisions interact rather than simply switching on and off.

4-4-7.title: Neuroplasticity
4-4-7.explanation: Neuroplasticity is the nervous system's capacity to change its structure or functioning in response to experience, learning, development or injury. Changes can involve synaptic strength, connections and functional reorganisation. Plasticity supports learning and recovery, but its extent and outcomes depend on age, experience, brain systems and the nature of injury.

4-10-1.title: Hunger
4-10-1.explanation: Hunger is a motivated state linked to energy regulation and food seeking. Hypothalamic and brainstem systems integrate signals about energy availability, while hormones and gut signals (including ghrelin, leptin and insulin) influence appetite. Eating is also shaped by learning, emotion, culture and environmental cues, so it is not controlled by one centre alone.

4-10-2.title: Thirst
4-10-2.explanation: Thirst motivates fluid seeking and helps maintain osmotic and volume balance. Osmoreceptors detect changes in the concentration of body fluids, while signals related to blood volume and pressure also influence drinking. Osmotic thirst and hypovolemic thirst reflect different physiological disturbances, though both contribute to fluid regulation.

4-10-3.title: Sleep
4-10-3.explanation: Sleep is a recurring biological state involving altered consciousness, reduced responsiveness and characteristic brain activity. Circadian timing and homeostatic sleep pressure jointly regulate sleep; NREM and REM stages show different physiological and EEG patterns. Sleep supports restoration, memory and other cognitive functions, and is not simply passive inactivity.

4-10-4.title: Sex
4-10-4.explanation: Sexual motivation and behaviour reflect interacting biological, psychological and sociocultural influences. Hormones and neural systems contribute to sexual development and motivation, while learning, relationships, beliefs and context shape expression. Sexual response models describe phases or patterns of response; they should not be mistaken for universal accounts of every individual's experience.

5-9-2.title: Thorndike's learning theory
5-9-2.explanation: Thorndike's connectionism explains learning as the strengthening or weakening of stimulus–response connections through consequences and practice. The Law of Effect states that responses followed by satisfying consequences become more likely, whereas responses followed by discomfort become less likely. His puzzle-box studies helped establish an experimental approach to instrumental learning.

5-9-3.title: Guthrie's learning theory
5-9-3.explanation: Guthrie's contiguity theory proposes that a stimulus pattern paired with a movement can become associated with that movement; learning is often described as one-trial association. Repetition may improve performance by building or refining movement patterns rather than strengthening a response through reinforcement. This emphasis differs from Thorndike's Law of Effect.

5-9-4.title: Hull's learning theory
5-9-4.explanation: Hull's neobehaviourist theory explains behaviour through intervening variables such as drive, habit strength and incentive. Learning involves the formation of stimulus–response habits, while drive reduction can reinforce responses that satisfy biological needs. Hull's formal, quantitative approach differs from Guthrie's contiguity account and Thorndike's emphasis on satisfying consequences.

5-10-4.title: Acquisition
5-10-4.explanation: Acquisition is the initial learning phase in classical conditioning during which a conditioned stimulus is paired with an unconditioned stimulus and begins to elicit a conditioned response. The timing, contingency and number of pairings affect learning. Acquisition refers to development of the association, not the later disappearance or return of a response.

5-10-5.title: Extinction and spontaneous recovery
5-10-5.explanation: Extinction occurs when a conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus, causing the conditioned response to weaken. Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished conditioned response after a rest interval. Extinction generally indicates new inhibitory learning, not necessarily erasure of the original association.

5-10-7.title: Higher-order conditioning
5-10-7.explanation: Higher-order conditioning occurs when a previously established conditioned stimulus is paired with a new neutral stimulus, which then acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response. The new stimulus is conditioned through its relation to the existing conditioned stimulus rather than direct pairing with the original unconditioned stimulus. Response strength may be weaker at higher orders.

5-10-8.title: Conditioning procedures
5-10-8.explanation: Classical conditioning procedures include delay, trace, simultaneous and backward arrangements of conditioned and unconditioned stimuli. In delay conditioning, the conditioned stimulus begins before and overlaps the unconditioned stimulus; trace conditioning inserts a gap; simultaneous conditioning presents them together; backward conditioning presents the unconditioned stimulus first. Contiguity and predictive relation influence effectiveness.

5-11-4.title: Law of Effect
5-11-4.explanation: Thorndike's Law of Effect states that responses followed by satisfying consequences become more likely in similar situations, whereas responses followed by annoying consequences become less likely. It provided a foundation for instrumental and operant learning. The law concerns how consequences alter response probability, not stimulus–stimulus pairing in classical conditioning.

5-11-5.title: Operant conditioning
5-11-5.explanation: Operant conditioning is learning in which the consequences of behaviour alter the future probability of that behaviour. Reinforcement increases behaviour; punishment decreases it. Positive means a stimulus is added and negative means one is removed, so positive/negative are not synonyms for good/bad. Schedules of reinforcement influence response patterns.

5-14-3.explanation: Observational learning involves acquiring behaviour by watching a model and the consequences of the model's actions. Learning can occur without immediate performance; vicarious reinforcement influences whether an observed behaviour is enacted.

5-18-9.title: Atkinson-Shiffrin model
5-18-9.explanation: The Atkinson–Shiffrin model distinguishes sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory as information-processing stores. Sensory memory briefly retains incoming sensory traces; attention allows selected information into short-term storage; rehearsal and encoding support longer-term retention. The model is a broad multi-store account, not a detailed component model of working memory.

5-18-10.title: Baddeley's working-memory model
5-18-10.explanation: Baddeley's working-memory model treats short-term memory as an active system for temporarily holding and manipulating information. The central executive controls attention; the phonological loop handles verbal/auditory material; the visuospatial sketchpad handles visual-spatial material; the episodic buffer integrates information across systems and long-term memory. This differs from a passive, unitary short-term store.

6-4-6.title: Heuristics
6-4-6.explanation: Heuristics are efficient mental shortcuts used to make judgments or solve problems with limited time or information. They reduce cognitive effort but can produce systematic errors. Availability relies on ease of recall; representativeness relies on similarity to a prototype; anchoring uses an initial value as a reference. A heuristic is not necessarily irrational in every context.

6-4-7.title: Means-end analysis
6-4-7.explanation: Means–end analysis solves a problem by comparing the current state with the goal state, identifying the difference and selecting an operator that reduces it. Subgoals may be created when the final goal cannot be reached directly. It is a deliberate search strategy, unlike insight, which involves a sudden restructuring of the problem.

6-4-8.title: Working backward
6-4-8.explanation: Working backward is a problem-solving strategy that starts with the desired goal and identifies the steps or conditions that must precede it. The solver then moves from the goal toward the initial state to construct a feasible sequence. It is useful when the goal state is clearer than the route forward.

6-4-9.title: Analogy
6-4-9.explanation: Analogy supports problem solving by mapping relevant relations from a familiar source problem onto a new target problem. Successful transfer depends on recognising structural similarity rather than superficial resemblance. The solver must identify corresponding elements and adapt the solution; an analogy can mislead when the underlying relations differ.

6-4-10.title: Insight
6-4-10.explanation: Insight is a sudden reorganisation of how a problem is represented, leading to an apparent immediate solution. Gestalt accounts emphasise restructuring and seeing relationships in a new way. Insight differs from gradual trial-and-error search, although prior knowledge and preparation may contribute to the solution.

6-4-11.title: Problem representation
6-4-11.explanation: Problem representation is the way a solver mentally defines the initial state, goal state, available operators and constraints. An incomplete or inaccurate representation can prevent progress even when relevant knowledge is available. Reframing the problem can reveal new operators or remove assumptions that unnecessarily restrict solutions.

6-4-12.title: Mental set and functional fixedness
6-4-12.explanation: A mental set is a tendency to use a familiar strategy because it worked previously, even when another approach would be better. Functional fixedness is a narrower tendency to see an object only in its customary function. Both constrain flexible problem representation, but functional fixedness specifically concerns perceived object use.

6-9-1.title: Types of decision-making
6-9-1.explanation: Decision-making involves selecting among alternatives in light of goals, preferences, information and constraints. Decisions may be individual or group-based, routine or novel, and made under certainty, risk or uncertainty. The classification depends on the decision context; a decision is not the same as problem solving, although the processes overlap.

6-9-2.title: Decision-making models
6-9-2.explanation: Decision-making models describe how alternatives are generated, evaluated and selected. Normative models specify how an ideally rational decision should be made; descriptive models explain how people actually decide, including limits on information and cognitive resources. Models may emphasise expected outcomes, sequential stages or simplifying strategies.

7-2-10.title: Cattell's trait approach
7-2-10.explanation: Cattell used factor analysis to identify source traits underlying observable surface traits and developed the 16 Personality Factor (16PF) model. His approach combined lexical and statistical methods to reduce many descriptors to a smaller set of dimensions. Cattell's sixteen-factor account should not be confused with the five-factor model.

7-2-11.title: Eysenck's trait approach
7-2-11.explanation: Eysenck proposed a hierarchical trait model with broad dimensions, most prominently Extraversion, Neuroticism and Psychoticism (PEN). He linked traits to biological and temperamental differences and used factor-analytic methods. The PEN model is a three-dimensional account, distinct from both Cattell's 16PF and the Big Five.

7-2-12.title: Big Five model
7-2-12.explanation: The Big Five model organises personality into Openness to Experience, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism (OCEAN). Each is a broad dimension with individuals varying along a continuum. The model is descriptive and trait-based; it does not claim that every person belongs to one discrete personality type.

7-4-7.title: Primary and secondary motives
7-4-7.explanation: Primary motives are commonly linked to biological needs essential for survival or physiological regulation, such as hunger, thirst and sleep. Secondary motives are acquired through learning and social experience, such as achievement, affiliation, power and approval. The distinction concerns origins and functions; learned motives can become highly influential.

7-4-8.title: Maslow's hierarchy of needs
7-4-8.explanation: Maslow's hierarchy proposes that human motivation includes physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem and self-actualisation needs, often represented as a hierarchy. Lower-level needs tend to demand attention when strongly deprived, while higher growth needs can guide behaviour. The hierarchy is a theoretical framework, not a rigid sequence followed identically by everyone.

7-16-7.title: Eustress and distress
7-16-7.explanation: Eustress refers to stress experienced as manageable or motivating, whereas distress refers to stress appraised as unpleasant, overwhelming or harmful. The distinction concerns the person's appraisal and consequences, not simply the presence or absence of physiological arousal. The same demand may be experienced differently by different people.

7-16-8.title: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome
7-16-8.explanation: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome describes a general physiological response to prolonged stress in three stages: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. Alarm is the initial mobilisation; resistance reflects continued adaptation; exhaustion may occur when resources are depleted. The model describes a general response pattern, not the psychological appraisal of a particular stressor.

7-16-9.title: Cognitive appraisal of stress
7-16-9.explanation: Cognitive appraisal accounts explain stress through how a person evaluates a demand and their coping resources. In Lazarus's framework, primary appraisal concerns whether an event is irrelevant, benign-positive or stressful; secondary appraisal evaluates what can be done. Reappraisal updates the evaluation as circumstances or resources change.

7-16-10.title: Problem-focused and emotion-focused coping
7-16-10.explanation: Problem-focused coping aims to change the stressor or the person's relationship to its practical demands; emotion-focused coping aims to regulate emotional distress. The usefulness of each depends on controllability and context. They can be used together, and neither category is universally superior.

7-18-1.title: Seligman's Explanatory styles
7-18-1.explanation: Seligman's explanatory style concerns habitual ways of explaining positive and negative events, often described along permanence, pervasiveness and personalisation dimensions. A pessimistic style tends to explain bad events as lasting, broad and personal; an optimistic style tends to make more temporary, specific and less self-blaming explanations. Explanatory style is related to learned helplessness but is not identical to it.

8-3-8.title: Fundamental attribution error
8-3-8.explanation: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overemphasise personal dispositions and underemphasise situational influences when explaining another person's behaviour. It concerns explanations of others; its strength varies with context and culture. It differs from self-serving bias, which protects or enhances one's self-evaluation.

8-3-11.explanation: The tripartite model describes attitudes through affective (feelings), behavioural (action tendencies) and cognitive (beliefs) components. 8-3-12.title: Cognitive dissonance and attitude change
8-3-12.explanation: Cognitive dissonance is an aversive state arising from inconsistency among cognitions or between beliefs and behaviour. People may reduce dissonance by changing an attitude, changing behaviour, adding consonant cognitions or trivialising the inconsistency. Attitude change is one possible reduction strategy, not the only one.

8-3-15.title: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
8-3-15.explanation: The bystander effect is the finding that an individual may be less likely to help when other people are present. Diffusion of responsibility is one explanation: each bystander feels less personal responsibility because others could act. Noticing the event, interpreting it as an emergency and knowing how to help also affect intervention.

8-5-2.explanation: Biological approaches explain aggression through interacting genetic, neural, hormonal and evolutionary influences. Biological factors influence propensity but do not make aggressive behaviour inevitable or independent of context.

8-5-3.title: Frustration-aggression hypothesis
8-5-3.explanation: The frustration–aggression hypothesis proposes a relationship between blocked goal-directed behaviour and aggressive responses. Later formulations treat frustration as one possible source of negative affect that can increase readiness for aggression, rather than a necessary and sufficient cause. Cues, learning, interpretation and situational conditions also matter.
